Building on rtailcat

Source: vignettes/building-on-rtailcat.qmd

rtailcat gives you TCP streams and UDP datagrams between two R processes that can be anywhere, without accounts, port forwarding, or a VPN. That is a low-level building block, so this vignette shows three small things you might build with it, each written as if it were a little package of its own:

  1. wormhole: send an R object or a file to someone else.
  2. remote: run R code on a machine behind a firewall, such as a lab workstation.
  3. progress: watch a long-running job report its progress, live, over UDP.

Each section first defines the functions and then shows them in use. The usage code always runs in two R sessions, usually on two different machines, and each code block is labeled with the machine it runs on. The code is complete and runnable; the functions are also installed with the package, and you can load them with

examples = system.file("examples", package = "rtailcat")
for (f in c("wormhole.R", "remote.R", "progress.R")) source(file.path(examples, f))

A tailcat address is a secret: anyone who has it can connect to the server. The output below shortens addresses to forms such as tcAbC...xYz, and where code needs an address you paste in the full one that the other side printed. Public keys (nodekey:...) are not secret, but they are shortened the same way.

The output shown was recorded by running the code against a local test relay. It is not computed when the vignette is built, because that needs two R sessions and a network connection.

Sending messages over a stream

A TCP connection is a stream of bytes, not of messages. $read() returns whatever has arrived, at most 64 KiB at a time, so one $write() on one side can turn into several reads on the other, and two writes can arrive in a single read. $read_all() collects everything up to the end of the stream, which is enough when each side sends one thing and then calls $close_write(). For a conversation with several messages in each direction you need to mark where each message ends.

$write_message() and $read_message() do this for you. Each $read_message() returns exactly what one $write_message() on the other side sent, however the bytes were split up on the way. It returns NULL when the other side has ended the stream between two messages, which is how a reader learns that the other side is done. With max_bytes it refuses a message larger than that before reading any of it, so a peer cannot make you allocate an arbitrary amount of memory. On the wire each message is its length as 4 bytes, big-endian, followed by the bytes, so a program written in another language can take part in the same conversation.

The examples below use messages for everything that goes over TCP. To send an R object, send serialize(x, NULL) as a message and call unserialize() on the other side.

wormhole: sending an object or a file

Sharing a data set with a collaborator usually means email attachments, a shared drive, or uploading it somewhere. With wormhole the sender runs wormhole_send(), which prints an address and waits; the receiver runs wormhole_receive() with that address and gets the object. Neither side needs a public IP address or an open port, and the data is encrypted end to end.

The sender starts a server, listens on a fixed port, and waits for one connection. It sends a small JSON header describing the payload, then the payload, and waits for the receiver to confirm before it shuts down. Once the receiver has connected, the listener is closed, so nobody else can connect with the same address.

wormhole_port = 4404L

wormhole_send = function(x, timeout = 600) {
  wormhole_offer(list(kind = "object"), serialize(x, NULL), timeout)
}

wormhole_send_file = function(path, timeout = 600) {
  payload = readBin(path, "raw", n = file.size(path))
  wormhole_offer(list(kind = "file", name = basename(path)), payload, timeout)
}

wormhole_offer = function(header, payload, timeout) {
  srv = TailcatServer$new()
  on.exit(srv$close(), add = TRUE)
  lst = srv$listen(wormhole_port)
  address = tailcat_reveal(srv$address)
  cli::cli_inform(c("Waiting for the receiver. Give them this address privately:", " " = "{address}"))

  conn = lst$accept(timeout = timeout)
  lst$close()
  header$size = length(payload)
  conn$write_message(jsonlite::toJSON(header, auto_unbox = TRUE), timeout = 60)
  conn$write_message(payload, timeout = timeout)
  reply = conn$read_message(timeout = timeout, as = "text", max_bytes = 16)
  if (!identical(reply, "ok")) {
    cli::cli_abort("The receiver did not confirm the transfer.")
  }
  conn$close()
  srv$close(drain = 5)
  cli::cli_inform("Sent {format_bytes(length(payload))}.")
  invisible(TRUE)
}

format_bytes = function(n) {
  format(structure(n, class = "object_size"), units = "auto", standard = "SI")
}

The address is a tailcat_secret, which prints as <redacted>, so wormhole_offer() calls tailcat_reveal() to show it deliberately. This is the one place the secret is meant to appear.

Closing a server tears down its connections at once, so the receiver might not see the end of the stream cleanly. Closing the connection first and then calling $close(drain = 5) waits up to five seconds for that shutdown to reach the other side before closing the server. The receiver does the same with its client.

The receiver dials the sender, reads the header and checks the announced size against its own limit, reads the payload, and only then confirms. A file is written to dir under the name the sender gave, after checking that the name cannot point anywhere else and that it would not overwrite an existing file.

wormhole_receive = function(address, dir = ".", max_bytes = 1e9, timeout = 600) {
  cl = TailcatClient$new(address)
  on.exit(cl$close(), add = TRUE)
  conn = cl$dial(wormhole_port, timeout = 60)
  header = conn$read_message(timeout = timeout, as = "text", max_bytes = 4096)
  if (is.null(header)) {
    cli::cli_abort("The sender closed the connection without sending anything.")
  }
  header = jsonlite::fromJSON(header)
  if (header$size > max_bytes) {
    cli::cli_abort("The sender offered {format_bytes(header$size)}, more than {.arg max_bytes} allows.")
  }
  what = if (header$kind == "file") header$name else "an R object"
  cli::cli_inform("Receiving {what} ({format_bytes(header$size)}).")
  payload = conn$read_message(timeout = timeout, max_bytes = header$size)
  if (is.null(payload)) {
    cli::cli_abort("The sender closed the connection before sending the data.")
  }

  value = if (header$kind == "file") wormhole_save(payload, header$name, dir) else unserialize(payload)
  conn$write_message("ok", timeout = 60)
  conn$close_write()
  conn$close()
  cl$close(drain = 5)
  value
}

wormhole_save = function(payload, name, dir) {
  if (!is.character(name) || length(name) != 1 || !nzchar(name) || name != basename(name) || name %in% c(".", "..")) {
    cli::cli_abort("The sender offered an unsafe file name.")
  }
  path = file.path(dir, name)
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.path {path}} already exists.")
  }
  writeBin(payload, path)
  path
}

unserialize() can run code while it rebuilds an object, so use wormhole_receive() for objects only from senders you trust. Here that is natural: the receiver connects to an address that the sender gave them, so they already know who is on the other end. Files are written as bytes and are not interpreted.

Using it

The sender passes any R object to wormhole_send(), which waits until the transfer is done.

library(rtailcat)
wormhole_send(mtcars)
#> Waiting for the receiver. Give them this address privately:
#>   tcAbC...xYz
#> Sent 3.8 kB.

The receiver pastes the address into wormhole_receive():

library(rtailcat)
cars = wormhole_receive("tcAbC...xYz")
#> Receiving an R object (3.8 kB).
head(cars, 3)
#>                mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
#> Mazda RX4     21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
#> Mazda RX4 Wag 21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
#> Datsun 710    22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1

Files work the same way. Each call starts a new server with a new address, so an address that was used once is worthless afterwards.

write.csv(mtcars, "mtcars.csv")
wormhole_send_file("mtcars.csv")
#> Waiting for the receiver. Give them this address privately:
#>   tcDeF...uVw
#> Sent 1.8 kB.
path = wormhole_receive("tcDeF...uVw")
#> Receiving mtcars.csv (1.8 kB).
path
#> [1] "./mtcars.csv"
nrow(read.csv(path))
#> [1] 32

remote: running R code on another machine

Suppose the data or the computing power you need sits on a workstation in your lab or office, behind a firewall that does not let you in. With remote, the workstation runs remote_serve(), and from anywhere you can send it R code to evaluate and get the results back.

This is much more powerful than sending a file, and so it needs more care. Anyone who can reach the server can run any R code on the host, so the host should accept only the clients it knows. tailcat supports this directly: each side can have a stable key pair, and a server given allowed_clients accepts connections only from those public keys. Stable keys also give the host a stable address, so the client can keep using it across restarts of the server.

tailcat_keygen(path) creates a key pair the first time and saves it in a file only you can read, and later calls load it from there. The file contains the private key and pre-shared key, so treat it like an SSH private key.

The host side accepts one connection at a time and handles requests on it until the client disconnects. Each request is a message holding a serialized R expression, evaluated in a fresh environment; the reply carries the value, any printed output, and the error message if evaluation failed.

remote_port = 4405L

remote_serve = function(keys, allowed_clients, max_bytes = 1e8) {
  srv = TailcatServer$new(key = keys, allowed_clients = allowed_clients)
  on.exit(srv$close(), add = TRUE)
  lst = srv$listen(remote_port)
  address = tailcat_reveal(srv$address)
  cli::cli_inform(c("Serving R for {length(allowed_clients)} client{?s} at this address:", " " = "{address}"))
  repeat {
    conn = lst$accept()
    cli::cli_inform("Client connected.")
    tryCatch(
      remote_session(conn, max_bytes),
      error = function(e) cli::cli_inform(c("The connection failed:", "x" = "{conditionMessage(e)}"))
    )
    conn$close()
  }
}

remote_session = function(conn, max_bytes) {
  n = 0
  repeat {
    request = conn$read_message(max_bytes = max_bytes)
    if (is.null(request)) {
      break
    }
    reply = remote_run(unserialize(request))
    conn$write_message(serialize(reply, NULL), timeout = 600)
    n = n + 1
  }
  cli::cli_inform("Client disconnected after {n} request{?s}.")
}

remote_run = function(expr) {
  env = new.env(parent = globalenv())
  result = list(value = NULL, visible = FALSE, error = NULL)
  result$output = utils::capture.output(
    tryCatch(
      {
        res = withVisible(eval(expr, env))
        result$value = res$value
        result$visible = res$visible
      },
      error = function(e) result$error <<- conditionMessage(e)
    )
  )
  result
}

On the client, remote_eval() sends an expression as written, and remote_call() sends a function together with arguments that are evaluated locally first. Printed output from the host is shown locally, and an error on the host becomes an error of class remote_error.

remote_connect = function(address, keys) {
  cl = TailcatClient$new(address, key = keys)
  conn = tryCatch(cl$dial(remote_port, timeout = 60), error = function(e) {
    cl$close()
    stop(e)
  })
  structure(list(client = cl, conn = conn), class = "remote_session")
}

remote_eval = function(session, expr, timeout = 600) {
  remote_request(session, substitute(expr), timeout)
}

remote_call = function(session, fun, ..., .timeout = 600) {
  remote_request(session, as.call(c(list(fun), list(...))), .timeout)
}

remote_request = function(session, expr, timeout, call = rlang::caller_env()) {
  session$conn$write_message(serialize(expr, NULL), timeout = timeout)
  reply = session$conn$read_message(timeout = timeout)
  if (is.null(reply)) {
    cli::cli_abort("The host closed the connection.", call = call)
  }
  result = unserialize(reply)
  if (length(result$output) > 0) {
    cat(result$output, sep = "\n")
  }
  if (!is.null(result$error)) {
    cli::cli_abort(c("The code failed on the host.", "x" = "{result$error}"), class = "remote_error", call = call)
  }
  if (result$visible) result$value else invisible(result$value)
}

remote_close = function(session) {
  session$conn$close_write()
  session$conn$close()
  session$client$close(drain = 5)
  invisible()
}

print.remote_session = function(x, ...) {
  cat(if (x$conn$is_closed) "<remote session, closed>" else "<remote session, connected>", "\n")
  invisible(x)
}

A function sent with remote_call() is serialized with its environment. A function defined at the top level of your session refers to the global environment, which is not sent, so on the host it sees the host’s global environment instead of your variables; pass what it needs as arguments.

Using it

The client creates its keys once and gives its public key to whoever runs the host. A public key is not a secret.

library(rtailcat)
keys = tailcat_keygen("~/.config/remote/client.json")
keys$public_key
#> [1] "nodekey:3f1c...9a0e"

The host does the same for itself and starts serving, allowing only that client. remote_serve() runs until it is interrupted, so run it in a dedicated R session, for example inside tmux or screen on the workstation. Thanks to the stable keys, its address stays the same every time it is restarted.

library(rtailcat)
keys = tailcat_keygen("~/.config/remote/host.json")
remote_serve(keys, allowed_clients = "nodekey:3f1c...9a0e")
#> Serving R for 1 client at this address:
#>   tcAbC...xYz
#> Client connected.
#> Warning: cannot open file 'no-such-file.csv': No such file or directory
#> Client disconnected after 5 requests.

The client connects with the host’s address and its own keys, then sends code. Each call is one round trip over the same connection.

r = remote_connect("tcAbC...xYz", keys)
remote_eval(r, summary(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars))$r.squared)
#> [1] 0.7528328
remote_call(r, function(n) {
  set.seed(1)
  x = rowMeans(matrix(rexp(n * 10), ncol = 10))
  cat("Simulated", n, "means on the host\n")
  round(quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975)), 3)
}, 1e6)
#> Simulated 1e+06 means on the host
#>  2.5% 97.5% 
#> 0.480 1.707 
remote_eval(r, assign("x", 1))
remote_eval(r, exists("x"))
#> [1] FALSE

The last two calls show that each request runs in a fresh environment: x does not survive from one request to the next. Errors on the host arrive as errors on the client, and the connection stays usable. Only printed output and errors are sent back; warnings and messages stay on the host, like the warning from read.csv() in the host’s output above.

remote_eval(r, read.csv("no-such-file.csv"))
#> Error in `remote_eval()`:
#> ! The code failed on the host.
#> ✖ cannot open the connection
remote_close(r)

A client whose key is not in allowed_clients cannot connect at all, even with the right address: its remote_connect() runs out its timeout. To allow another client while the host is running, call $allow_client() on the server; here that would mean adding an argument to remote_serve() or reading the allowed keys from a file.

remote_serve() handles one client at a time, and while it evaluates a request it does nothing else. That is fine for one person using their own workstation. Several users, or several requests in parallel, would call for one worker process per connection, for example with callr or mirai, but the protocol would stay the same.

progress: watching a long-running job over UDP

A long simulation or model fit on a cluster node or a cloud machine usually reports its progress to a log file, which you then have to go and read. With progress, the job sends small progress reports to your laptop as it runs, and your laptop collects them in the background, while you keep using the R console, or shows them in a Shiny app.

This is a good fit for UDP. Each report is a single small datagram, and if one is lost the next one is along shortly, so there is no point in waiting for retransmissions or keeping a connection alive. More importantly, sending a datagram never blocks the job for long and never fails because the monitor has gone away: the job should not slow down, or stop, because nobody is watching. Each datagram holds at most 1232 bytes, which is plenty for a few numbers encoded as JSON.

Note that the server runs on the laptop and the job is the client, the reverse of what you might expect. The laptop prints an address and the job dials it, so neither needs to accept connections from the internet.

The monitor listens on a UDP port and calls a handler for each flow, one per job. The handler starts a read loop on the flow, which calls progress_record() with each datagram as it arrives. Nothing blocks: the reports are collected by the later event loop whenever the R console is idle, or while Shiny is running.

progress_monitor = function(port = 9000L) {
  srv = TailcatServer$new()
  lst = srv$listen(port, network = "udp")
  monitor = new.env(parent = emptyenv())
  monitor$server = srv
  monitor$events = list()
  lst$serve(function(conn) {
    conn$read_loop(function(datagram) progress_record(monitor, datagram), on_error = function(e) NULL)
  })
  address = tailcat_reveal(srv$address)
  cli::cli_inform(c("Collecting progress reports on UDP port {port}. Address for the jobs:", " " = "{address}"))
  structure(monitor, class = "progress_monitor")
}

progress_record = function(monitor, datagram) {
  event = tryCatch(jsonlite::fromJSON(rawToChar(datagram)), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.list(event)) {
    event$received = Sys.time()
    monitor$events[[length(monitor$events) + 1]] = event
  }
  invisible()
}

progress_data = function(monitor) {
  events = monitor$events
  if (length(events) == 0) {
    return(data.frame())
  }
  cols = unique(unlist(lapply(events, names)))
  rows = lapply(events, function(e) {
    e[setdiff(cols, names(e))] = NA
    as.data.frame(e[cols])
  })
  out = do.call(rbind, rows)
  out = out[order(out$job, out$seq), , drop = FALSE]
  rownames(out) = NULL
  out
}

progress_stop = function(monitor) {
  monitor$server$close()
  invisible()
}

print.progress_monitor = function(x, ...) {
  jobs = unique(vapply(x$events, function(e) e$job, character(1)))
  cat("<progress monitor>", length(x$events), "reports from", length(jobs), "jobs\n")
  invisible(x)
}

A report that is malformed, for example one sent by something other than progress_report(), is ignored. Since a monitor accepts reports from anyone who has its address, it does nothing with them other than store them. If reading from a flow fails, the read loop closes it; the on_error callback that does nothing keeps that from showing up as a warning.

The job side dials the monitor once and then sends one datagram per report. Each report carries the job name and a sequence number, so the monitor can tell jobs apart and notice lost reports. progress_report() never signals an error: if the monitor is unreachable the report is simply lost, and a write that cannot complete within a second is abandoned.

progress_reporter = function(address, job, port = 9000L) {
  cl = TailcatClient$new(address)
  reporter = new.env(parent = emptyenv())
  reporter$client = cl
  reporter$conn = cl$dial(port, network = "udp", timeout = 60)
  reporter$job = job
  reporter$seq = 0L
  reporter
}

progress_report = function(reporter, ...) {
  reporter$seq = reporter$seq + 1L
  event = list(job = reporter$job, seq = reporter$seq, sent = as.numeric(Sys.time()), ...)
  payload = charToRaw(jsonlite::toJSON(event, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA))
  if (length(payload) > tailcat_udp_max_payload()) {
    cli::cli_warn("Report {reporter$seq} is {length(payload)} bytes, over the {tailcat_udp_max_payload()} bytes a datagram can hold, and was not sent.")
    return(invisible(FALSE))
  }
  sent = tryCatch(
    {
      reporter$conn$write(payload, timeout = 1)
      TRUE
    },
    error = function(e) FALSE
  )
  invisible(sent)
}

progress_done = function(reporter) {
  reporter$client$close()
  invisible()
}

Finally, a small Shiny app plots one metric against another, with a line per job, and lists each job’s latest report. It checks for new reports once a second. Shiny runs the later event loop, so the monitor keeps collecting reports while the app is open.

progress_app = function(monitor, x = "iter", y = "loss") {
  ui = shiny::fluidPage(
    shiny::titlePanel("Job progress"),
    shiny::plotOutput("plot"),
    shiny::tableOutput("latest")
  )
  server = function(input, output, session) {
    data = shiny::reactivePoll(
      1000, session,
      checkFunc = function() length(monitor$events),
      valueFunc = function() progress_data(monitor)
    )
    output$plot = shiny::renderPlot({
      d = data()
      shiny::req(nrow(d) > 0, x %in% names(d), y %in% names(d))
      jobs = unique(d$job)
      plot(d[[x]], d[[y]], type = "n", xlab = x, ylab = y)
      for (i in seq_along(jobs)) {
        rows = d$job == jobs[i]
        lines(d[[x]][rows], d[[y]][rows], col = i, lwd = 2)
      }
      legend("topright", legend = jobs, col = seq_along(jobs), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
    })
    output$latest = shiny::renderTable({
      d = data()
      shiny::req(nrow(d) > 0)
      latest = d[!duplicated(d$job, fromLast = TRUE), setdiff(names(d), c("sent", "received")), drop = FALSE]
      latest$age = paste(round(as.double(Sys.time() - d$received[!duplicated(d$job, fromLast = TRUE)], units = "secs")), "s")
      latest
    })
  }
  shiny::shinyApp(ui, server)
}

Using it

Start the monitor on your laptop. It returns at once and keeps collecting in the background.

library(rtailcat)
m = progress_monitor()
#> Collecting progress reports on UDP port 9000. Address for the jobs:
#>   tcAbC...xYz

Give the job the address, for example through an environment variable, or a file only you can read written with tailcat_address_write(m$server, path) and read in the job with tailcat_address_read(path), and call progress_report() wherever the job has something to say. Here a loop that shrinks a number stands in for the real work.

library(rtailcat)
reporter = progress_reporter("tcAbC...xYz", job = "fit-1")
loss = 1
for (i in 1:20) {
  Sys.sleep(0.1)
  loss = loss * 0.8
  progress_report(reporter, iter = i, loss = loss)
}
progress_done(reporter)

Back on the laptop the reports have arrived. Missing sequence numbers would show lost reports.

m
#> <progress monitor> 20 reports from 1 jobs
d = progress_data(m)
tail(d[c("job", "seq", "iter", "loss")], 3)
#>      job seq iter       loss
#> 18 fit-1  18   18 0.01801440
#> 19 fit-1  19   19 0.01441152
#> 20 fit-1  20   20 0.01152922
setdiff(seq_len(max(d$seq)), d$seq)
#> integer(0)

While jobs are running, progress_app() shows their progress live. Any number of jobs can report to one monitor, each under its own name.

shiny::runApp(progress_app(m))
progress_stop(m)

The monitor’s address changes every time it starts. To keep one address for all your jobs, create keys once with tailcat_keygen(path), which saves them securely and loads them on later calls, and pass them to TailcatServer$new(key = keys) in progress_monitor(), as remote_serve() does.

In an R script run with Rscript, rather than at the console, nothing runs the event loop while the script waits, so call tailcat_run() to keep collecting reports, for example tailcat_run(timeout = 3600) for an hour.
